bio.en: Chris Miller is VP of Product for Growth and AI at HubSpot, where he helped create the company's early growth team and turned it into one of the most successful product-led growth businesses in history.
bio.zh: Chris Miller 是 HubSpot 增长与 AI 产品副总裁，他曾帮助创建公司的早期增长团队，并将其打造成史上最成功的产品驱动增长业务之一。

summary.en: Chris covers what it takes to become a successful product leader, the skills the best PMs build, and how to find mentors early in your career. He emphasizes radical ownership and accountability—treating every problem as yours—as the mindset that helped HubSpot's growth team find opportunities others missed. The conversation also stresses why early PMs must “scrape their knees” to learn.
summary.zh: Chris 涵盖了成为成功产品领导者需要什么、顶尖 PM 培养的技能，以及职业生涯早期如何找到导师。他强调“彻底的拥有感与责任感”——把每个问题都当成自己的——这一心态帮助 HubSpot 增长团队发现别人错过的机会。对话还强调早期 PM 必须“摔跟头”才能学到东西。

turns.speaker: Chris Miller
turns.en: ... The actual really small initial growth team. We really had an aggressive mentality, an aggressive approach, and what that looked like was at the time, a very small percentage of, I think HubSpot's subscription revenue would be described as self-service, so we approached the team who owned it and we were like, "Are you all working on this?" They were like, "Nah, we're working on a bunch of other stuff." We were like, "Can we take this?" They were like, "Sure, if you want it." And so, we took it and immediately blew it up, and so that attitude of saying that every problem is our problem and radical accountability and ownership mentality helped us find opportunities that maybe the business wasn't explicitly asking us to solve, but we were able to triangulate why it might be important for the business for us to solve it. When you do that, we look hungry, so let's keep feeding us, right?
turns.zh: ...实际上非常小的初始增长团队。我们确实有一种积极进取的心态，一种积极进取的方法，当时看起来，我认为 HubSpot 的订阅收入中的一小部分可以被描述为自助服务，所以我们联系了拥有它的团队，我们说，“你们都在做这个吗？”他们的反应是，“不，我们正在做很多其他的事情。”我们当时想，“我们可以接受这个吗？”他们说：“当然，如果你想要的话。”因此，我们接受了它并立即将其炸毁，因此说每个问题都是我们的问题的态度以及激进的问责制和所有权心态帮助我们找到了机会，也许企业没有明确要求我们解决，但我们能够三角测量为什么我们解决它对企业可能很重要。当你这样做时，我们看起来很饿，所以让我们继续喂我们吧？

turns.speaker: Chris Miller
turns.en: I've been leading PLG at HubSpot for several years now, and I recently took on the AI leadership role. It's a special place to be in and that I get to help lead HubSpot in terms of how we should be thinking about building the foundational technology to create AI-powered experiences and then also lead the strategy of how we leverage those experiences to help that B2B business builder be way more successful using our platform than they might've been in years past. turns.zh: 我在 HubSpot 领导 PLG 已经好几年了，最近我又担任了 AI 领导职务。这是一个特殊的地方，我可以帮助领导 HubSpot 思考如何构建基础技术来创造人工智能驱动的体验，然后领导我们如何利用这些经验来帮助 B2B 业务创建者使用我们的平台比过去几年更成功的战略。所以，这是这两件事之间非常酷的交叉点。我们可以在那里做很多事情。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One thing I took away from what you just shared is that you are given these two teams to lead, which aren't necessarily connected, but I think it tells me that you're doing a great job at HubSpot and I'm going to try to pierce through your modesty and I'm curious, what is it that you think you've done really well or been successful at that got the leaders at HubSpot to decide to give you this other team that feels like an incredibly important initiative in this time of AI?
turns.zh: 我从你刚才分享的内容中学到的一件事是，你被赋予了这两个团队来领导，这两个团队没有必然的联系，但我认为这告诉我，你在 HubSpot 做得很好，我将尝试戳破你的谦虚，我很好奇，你认为自己在哪些方面做得很好或取得了成功，让 HubSpot 的领导者决定给你另一个团队，这在人工智能时代感觉是一个非常重要的举措？

turns.speaker: Chris Miller
turns.en: So when I joined HubSpot in 2016, it was definitely an element of timing that really worked in my favor. It was maybe like a year or so after HubSpot had launched their free CRM, which was a big strategic play for them and for us, excuse me, at the time, and it was meant to be disruptive, but I don't think that there was a fully formed perspective on what was going to happen after that. How are we actually going to get leverage and enterprise value out of this sort of big, enormous piece of free software we just put into the universe? And I think the pedigree of product manager at HubSpot at that time was also a bit different. There were folks who maybe started their time at HubSpot in support, and so intimately familiar with the product and with customers. Some of these people had closed thousands of support tickets and my background was a bit different. (00:06:57): I was actually less of a feature PM and I was sort of more of a growth PM in my DNA, and so I sort of looked at this through a completely different lens and I guess I understood that what we were trying to actually do was product-led growth, but we didn't really have the shared vocabulary to call it that. And so I think to answer your question, I think I was just willing to take some risks and really push for the things that I believed made sense even though maybe based on the titles that I had at the time, I wasn't sort of inherently given a seat at the table and really pushed my away into some of these conversations and then was eventually invited to them. And so, just always had an interest in driving a strategy that was a click or two higher than maybe what my immediate team was focused on and was always curious about how other parts of the business functioned. (00:07:51): I used to spend a lot of time sitting on the sales floor, just going into the other buildings and talking to other folks, working on different parts of the business, and that's part of maybe the serendipity that I miss about being in person, which is that you might just discover something from having a casual conversation with someone at the water cooler. You're like, "Oh, that's an interesting problem. I think my team can help with that," so you absorb a bunch of context around how pieces of the business are connected and you can start to really widen your aperture in terms of the size of opportunities that might be in front of you that maybe you would've missed if you would've been so heads down on execution work. And so, if I had to guess how people might talk about that, if I wasn't in the room, maybe they would cite that, but it's tough to say.
turns.zh: 因此，当我在 2016 年加入 HubSpot 时，时机确实对我有利。大概是在 HubSpot 推出免费 CRM 一年左右之后，对不起，当时这对他们和我们来说都是一次重大的战略行动，它本来是具有颠覆性的，但我认为对于之后会发生的事情还没有一个完全形成的观点。我们实际上如何从我们刚刚投入宇宙的这种巨大的自由软件中获得影响力和企业价值？而且我觉得当时HubSpot的产品经理的血统也有点不一样。有些人可能是从 HubSpot 开始从事支持工作的，因此对产品和客户非常熟悉。其中一些人已经关闭了数千张支持请求，而我的背景有点不同。 (00:06:57)：实际上，在我的基因里，我并不是一个功能产品经理，而是一个增长产品经理，所以我从一个完全不同的角度来看待这个问题，我想我明白我们实际上想做的是产品主导的增长，但我们并没有真正拥有共同的词汇来称呼它。所以我想回答你的问题，我想我只是愿意冒一些风险，真正推动我认为有意义的事情，尽管也许基于我当时拥有的头衔，我本质上并没有在谈判桌上占有一席之地，而是真正把我推到了其中一些对话中，然后最终被邀请参加它们。因此，我总是有兴趣推动比我的直属团队关注的内容高一两次点击的策略，并且总是对业务其他部分的运作方式感到好奇。 (00:07:51)：我曾经花很多时间坐在销售楼层，只是走进其他建筑物并与其他人交谈，从事业务的不同部分，这可能是我怀念面对面的机缘的一部分，即你可能会在饮水机旁与某人随意交谈时发现一些东西。你会说，“哦，这是一个有趣的问题。我认为我的团队可以帮助解决这个问题”，因此你吸收了一系列有关业务各个部分如何相互关联的背景信息，并且你可以开始真正扩大你的视野，了解可能摆在你面前的机会的大小，如果你一直埋头于执行工作，你可能会错过这些机会。因此，如果我不得不猜测人们会如何谈论这一点，如果我不在房间里，也许他们会引用这一点，但这很难说。

turns.speaker: Chris Miller

So definitely a lot of upside, but certainly you got to be a little bit more creative in terms of that serendipitous knowledge sharing, the osmosis learning, and just context sharing that happens more organically when everybody's sharing the same physical space.
turns.zh: 是的，一切都安排得如此紧凑，你从一个 Zoom 跳到另一个 Zoom，显然 HubSpot 已经接受了混合，并且它有很多好处。事实上，当我回到工作岗位时，我是一个新爸爸，而我的儿子不在日托所，所以能够在会议间隙抽出时间和他一起玩几分钟然后回去真是太酷了，而当你一整天都在办公室时，你就无法体会到这一点。所以肯定有很多好处，但当然，在偶然的知识共享、渗透学习以及当每个人共享相同的物理空间时更有机地发生的上下文共享方面，你必须更具创造力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You talked about how some of your early success was taking risks and being in meetings maybe you shouldn't be in. turns.speaker: Chris Miller
turns.en: This is a funny story. For anybody at HubSpot listening, I apologize in retrospect for this, but-
turns.zh: 这是一个有趣的故事。对于 HubSpot 收听的任何人，我对此表示歉意，但是——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm excited for this.
turns.zh: 我对此感到很兴奋。

turns.speaker: Chris Miller
turns.en: There was a time where we were having a lot of debates around pricing and packaging, and we'll get into this, but our go-to-market model and sort of where we play in the addressable market created some complexity in the sense of we're serving different parts of the market simultaneously with the connected unified platform. And so, how do you think about packaging and go-to-market? And we were trying to just figure out how to simplify, simplify, simplify. And at the time I was an IC, individual contributing PM, so who am I to have a point of view on pricing and packaging? But the person I was working with, my designer, her name's Mariah Moscato, she's in product now, she's excellent, we were part of a triad and we both had a similar school of thought in terms of what the pricing packaging could be. (00:10:33): And we were over in Dublin where we have our European headquarters and there was a party happening at the Guinness sort of storehouse, and I don't know that we were exactly on the guest list, but we figured out a way to get into the party and we ran into the COO at the time and out of the blue I think he had asked us what we thought about pricing and packaging and it was sort of one of those funny you should ask moments. And so, we ended up kind of pitching in the midst of pints being sort of handed every which way you could turn this vision for a completely different way we might approach pricing and packaging, and he was pretty intrigued and he said, "Why don't you come to the next executive meeting and pitch us on it?" (00:11:22): I think that meeting was maybe a couple of weeks away and so we looked at each other and we were like, "Uh-oh," not exactly what we expected in terms of, I think people welcoming maybe a contrarian point of view at that moment in time. And so, we sort of were invited into this meeting with folks that we generally don't get to spend a lot of time with to pitch this thing that swam a little bit upstream and we ultimately didn't go full steam ahead down that path. I think a lot of elements of what we pitched have made their way over time into HubSpot's pricing and packaging, but it certainly I think opened the door for us and for me, speaking for myself, certainly for me to be welcomed back into that room in the future and to be able to contribute ideas towards important decisions.
turns.zh: 有一段时间，我们围绕定价和包装进行了很多争论，我们将对此进行讨论，但我们的上市模式以及我们在目标市场中的定位造成了一些复杂性，因为我们通过连接的统一平台同时为市场的不同部分提供服务。那么，您如何看待包装和上市？我们试图弄清楚如何简化、简化、再简化。当时我是一名 IC、个人贡献 PM，那么我有什么资格对定价和包装发表观点呢？但和我一起工作的人，我的设计师，她的名字叫玛丽亚·莫斯卡托，她现在正在生产产品，她很优秀，我们是黑社会的一部分，我们在定价包装方面有着相似的思想流派。 (00:10:33)：我们在都柏林，我们有我们的欧洲总部，在吉尼斯之类的仓库里举办了一场派对，我不知道我们到底在客人名单上，但我们找到了一种进入派对的方法，当时我们遇到了首席运营官，我想他突然问了我们对定价和包装的看法，这是你应该问的有趣时刻之一。因此，我们最终在各种方式进行推销，你可以将这一愿景转变为一种完全不同的方式，我们可能会处理定价和包装，他很感兴趣，他说，“你为什么不来参加下一次执行会议并向我们推销呢？” (00:11:22)：我认为会议可能还有几周的时间，所以我们互相看着对方，然后我们说，“哦，”这并不完全符合我们的预期，我认为人们在那一刻可能会欢迎逆向观点。因此，我们被邀请参加这次会议，与我们通常不会花很多时间的人一起推销这个逆流而上的东西，我们最终没有沿着这条路全速前进。我认为，随着时间的推移，我们推销的很多元素已经融入到了 HubSpot 的定价和包装中，但我认为这无疑为我们和我打开了大门，为我自己说话，当然也为我在未来受到欢迎回到那个房间，并能够为重要决策贡献想法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. It's another example of serendipity and just running into people. Also, I think it's a really good example of just how important it's for PMs to be proactive and think ahead and not just rely on people coming to you, asking you for your advice and getting invited to rooms. I feel like so much of success in the product leadership role is just suggesting great ideas, being ahead of where people are and having the answers. You have the answer right there in the moment because you did the work ahead of time. Is that something you find as well that ends up being really important?
turns.zh: 我喜欢那个。这是机缘巧合和偶然相遇的另一个例子。另外，我认为这是一个很好的例子，说明了产品经理积极主动、超前思考的重要性，而不仅仅是依赖人们来找你、向你征求建议并被邀请到会议室。我觉得产品领导角色的成功只是提出了伟大的想法，走在人们的前面并找到了答案。你现在就已经有了答案，因为你提前完成了工作。您是否也发现这件事最终变得非常重要？

turns.speaker: Chris Miller
turns.en: Yeah, one of the traits that I look for in PMs that I hire onto my teams, and also when I think back to the people that I've learned a lot from working with over the years, one of the common behaviors or traits is relentless curiosity, this insatiable desire to understand things and a lack of fear in admitting when they don't understand things and being uncompromising and getting the answers so that they do understand. And I think if you can bring that to the table, it's much easier to have an outsized impact on whatever or you're a part of or whatever mission you're working on or whatever team you may be a member of.
turns.zh: 是的，我在团队中聘用的 PM 中寻找的特质之一，也是当我回想起这些年来与我一起工作的人时，他们的共同行为或特质之一是不懈的好奇心，这种对理解事物的永不满足的渴望，以及在承认他们不理解的事情时不畏惧，不妥协并得到答案，以便他们真正理解。我认为，如果你能把这一点摆到桌面上，那么就更容易对你参与的任何事情、你正在执行的任何任务或你可能所属的任何团队产生巨大的影响。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Are there any other traits on that list of traits you look for that you think are really important that maybe other people don't focus on?
turns.zh: 在您寻找的特征列表中是否还有其他您认为非常重要但其他人可能没有关注的特征？

turns.speaker: Chris Miller
turns.en: Yeah, relentless curiosity is probably my number one. My number two would probably be resilience, specifically if you're working in growth. I think if you're doing growth, right, if you're doing product-led growth the right way, then you're trying to balance the science and sort of taking a somewhat hygienic approach to validating assumptions and hypotheses with being really ambitious and really pushing for the things that are going to have massive impact for your customers at the end of the day. And when you're doing that, you're going to fail more than you're going to be successful along the way. And if you're not resilient, that can be really demotivating. I think there's a stat that some growth person put out there years ago, which is that on average only 20 to 30% of experiments of growth team runs might be successful. So, that means 70 to 80% of the time you're, you're not putting numbers on the board and you're extracting learnings hopefully that you can apply to the future. (00:14:43): But I think if you're not resilient, what I've seen happen is you end up sort of grasping for a win, which can sometimes look like making bets that are too small and too insignificant to matter. If your sort of primary modality of product-led growth work is experiment-driven product development and you're hitting more than like 30, 40% of the time, you're thinking too small. And so, that resiliency piece is certainly important in my mind. I think coachability is another one in the sense that I still think that the sort of subcategory of growth product management is still fledgling compared to PMs working on platform features. And so, even when I'm interviewing folks, I'm not necessarily looking for 10 years of experience doing PLG. I think that's mostly an unreasonable ask, but it can certainly be taught and even if you do have some experience doing PLG work, it's important to know that what that work is going to look like is going to potentially vary in a meaningful way from shop to shop. (00:15:49): And so, being coachable and adaptable to whatever the context is of the business or problem space that you're working on I think is an important trait that I look for in PMs, and then creativity is so important too. Valuing simple solutions to really hard problems, I think if building the next super sophisticated widget is the thing that gets you out of bed in the morning, growth might not be for you, I think the best growth product leaders and growth minds that I've worked with over the years or have had the privilege of learning from over the years, I think the thing that I noticed about them is they're almost ambivalent to the solution and certainly ambivalent to how complex a solution may or may not be. And taking little to no pleasure or pride in the complexity of a solution so long that it delivers the outcome that the business and your customers need, I think is a really cool trait, and I kind categorize that under creativity.
turns.zh: 是的，不懈的好奇心可能是我的第一要务。我的第二点可能是韧性，特别是如果你从事增长工作的话。我认为，如果你正在以正确的方式进行产品主导的增长，那么你就会试图在科学和采取某种卫生方法来验证假设和假说之间取得平衡，同时雄心勃勃，真正推动那些最终会对你的客户产生巨大影响的事情。当你这样做时，一路上你失败的次数会多于成功的次数。如果你没有韧性，那真的会让人失去动力。我认为一些增长人士几年前就曾公布过一项统计数据，即增长团队的实验平均只有 20% 到 30% 可能会成功。所以，这意味着 70% 到 80% 的时间里，你不是在黑板上写数字，而是在提取经验教训，希望可以应用到未来。 (00:14:43)：但我认为，如果你没有弹性，我所看到的情况就是你最终会抓住胜利，这有时看起来像是下的赌注太小、太微不足道，不重要。如果您以产品为主导的增长工作的主要方式是实验驱动的产品开发，并且您的成功率超过 30%、40%，那么您的想法就太小了。因此，在我看来，弹性部分当然很重要。我认为可指导性是另一种意义，因为我仍然认为与从事平台功能的产品经理相比，增长产品管理的子类别仍处于起步阶段。因此，即使我在面试人们，我也不一定会寻找拥有 10 年 PLG 经验的人。我认为这基本上是一个不合理的要求，但它肯定是可以教授的，即使您确实有一些从事 PLG 工作的经验，重要的是要知道这项工作的外观可能会因商店而异。 (00:15:49)：因此，我认为，能够接受指导并能够适应您正在处理的业务或问题空间的任何环境，是我在产品经理中寻找的一个重要特质，此外创造力也非常重要。重视对真正困难问题的简单解决方案，我认为如果构建下一个超级复杂的小部件是让你早上起床的事情，那么增长可能不适合你，我认为多年来与我共事或有幸向他们学习的最好的增长产品领导者和增长思想，我认为我注意到他们对解决方案几乎是矛盾的，当然对解决方案可能或可能不复杂的态度也很矛盾。只要解决方案能够提供业务和客户所需的结果，我就不会因为解决方案的复杂性而感到高兴或自豪，我认为这是一个非常酷的特质，我将其归类为创造力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You mentioned this phrase, relentless curiosity, and it made me think about a story I read about you where the way you got into product management was you were at some startup and the founder was just like, "I've read that the cure to all our problems is going to be hiring product manager," and you heard that and you googled, what is product management, and then you asked them, "Can I do that?" And that's how you got into the role. So first of all, is that true? And second of all, what's your advice to people trying to get into product management and any lessons from that experience?
turns.zh: 你提到了这句话，不懈的好奇心，这让我想起了我读过的一个关于你的故事，你进入产品管理的方式是你在一家初创公司，创始人就像是，“我读到解决我们所有问题的方法是雇用产品经理，”你听到这句话，你用谷歌搜索，什么是产品管理，然后你问他们，“我可以这样做吗？”这就是你进入这个角色的方式。那么首先，这是真的吗？其次，您对那些试图进入产品管理领域的人有什么建议，以及从这次经历中得到的教训是什么？

turns.speaker: Chris Miller
turns.en: So first, yes, that is 100% true. That is how I stumbled into product management. So, I appreciate all the folks who took a shot on me back then, but this was at a time where I would say product management even as a function was definitely not ubiquitous across tech. There was, at least in the world that I was in, a lot more of a standard waterfall approach to building product with a lot of middle layers and engineering managers and really no one who had the job of owning the problem from a customer's point of view. And so, there wasn't a ton of content out there. There weren't even a ton of people in the city at the time that I could really talk to sort of learn, and so a lot of what I did was scrape my knees through the first years and a lot of painful trial and error. (00:18:08): And then eventually I think there's a lot more energy and an interest around the trade craft and the function, and so I think it's much easier today for someone to learn the fundamentals of product management without necessarily needing to do it via trial by fire. My advice to folks who are interested in breaking into product management specifically is focus on a few things. One, focus on structure. I think there's usually a lower barrier to entry to do product management at a smaller shop, which they might not have as much access to the best talent out there, but I think what you may often give up in those instances is structure to your own sort of professional development and formal training and education and potentially even the opportunity to work for people who are truly battle tested and have seen the movie several times and can actually wisdom share because truthfully, it looks different in every company, and so it is one of those functions. (00:19:13): I do believe that taking a truly academic approach towards upskilling has fairly diminishing returns because it's tough to field curveballs in a classroom. And so, choosing where you want to break in is almost as important as choosing that you want to break in the first place. Thinking about who you're going to be reporting to, thinking about what's the track record of success for people at that company, breaking into product management, trying to think five years in advance and work backwards, I think are all sort of important thought exercises along the way. I would also say that if you're already at a shop where you are working at a different function and you're sort of product curious, go talk to the PMs, literally I say go reach out to a PM and ask how you can make their day easier. (00:20:01): Figure out what you can do in your spare time that they can offload to you and do a little bit of volunteer labor, even if that's just shadowing because I think just getting that context and understanding the sort of rhythm of how a team ideates and defines problems and prioritizes and ship software is the experience that's going to be the most important because a lot of product management is also managing personalities and figuring out how people want to work with you and figuring out how you work for them. And so, just getting that hands-on experience or at least direct sight-line into the day-to-day of a team is really important because the extent to which you can understand their problem space and understand the things that keep them up at night, you can be valuable, and then at the very least, what you get out of it is hopefully an advocate or a sponsor at the end of the day who is willing to gamble some professional and political capital on you to get your foot into the door even though you might not have any formal experience on your resume.
turns.zh: 首先，是的，这是 100% 正确的。这就是我偶然进入产品管理的原因。所以，我很感谢当时所有对我进行攻击的人，但在那个时候，我想说，产品管理即使作为一种功能，在整个技术领域也绝对不是普遍存在的。至少在我所处的世界里，有更多的标准瀑布方法来构建产品，有很多中间层和工程经理，而且实际上没有人负责从客户的角度来解决问题。因此，那里没有太多内容。当时城里甚至没有很多人可以让我真正交谈学习，所以我所做的很多事情都是在最初的几年里艰难地度过，并经历了很多痛苦的尝试和错误。 (00:18:08)：最终我认为人们对贸易工艺和功能有更多的精力和兴趣，所以我认为今天人们学习产品管理的基础知识要容易得多，而不必通过艰苦的试验来做到这一点。我对那些有兴趣进入产品管理领域的人的建议是关注一些事情。一是注重结构。我认为在较小的商店进行产品管理通常门槛较低，他们可能没有那么多机会接触到最优秀的人才，但我认为在这种情况下你可能经常放弃的是你自己的专业发展和正规培训和教育的结构，甚至可能放弃为那些真正经过战斗考验、看过电影多次并且实际上可以分享智慧的人工作的机会，因为说实话，每个公司看起来都不同，所以它是这些功能之一。 (00:19:13)：我确实相信，采取真正的学术方法来提高技能的回报会相当递减，因为在教室里打出曲线球是很困难的。因此，选择你想要闯入的地方几乎与选择你想要闯入的地方一样重要。思考你将向谁汇报，思考该公司员工的成功记录，进入产品管理领域，尝试提前五年思考并向后工作，我认为这些都是重要的思维练习。我还想说，如果你已经在一家商店从事不同的职能工作，并且你对产品有点好奇，那就去和产品经理谈谈，我说的是去联系产品经理，询问如何让他们的一天变得更轻松。 (00:20:01)：弄清楚你可以在业余时间做什么，他们可以分担给你，做一些志愿工作，即使这只是影子，因为我认为，了解背景并理解团队如何构思、定义问题、确定优先级和交付软件的节奏是最重要的体验，因为很多产品管理也在管理个性，弄清楚人们希望如何与你合作，并弄清楚你如何为他们工作。因此，获得实践经验或至少直接了解团队的日常工作非常重要，因为你能够在多大程度上了解他们的问题空间并了解让他们彻夜难眠的事情，你是有价值的，然后至少，你从中得到的希望是一天结束时的倡导者或赞助商，他们愿意在你身上赌上一些专业和政治资本，让你踏入大门，即使你的简历上可能没有任何正式的经验。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's so much stuff that super resonates there. One is that I always think of the bare minimum job of a PM is just to be useful to people on the team and help them do better work. If you do that alone, people-
turns.zh: 那里有很多能引起超级共鸣的东西。一是我一直认为 PM 最起码的工作就是对团队中的人有用并帮助他们做得更好。如果你单独做这件事，人们——

turns.speaker: Chris Miller
turns.en: Bring the donuts, right?
turns.zh: 带甜甜圈来吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Bring the donuts, exactly.
turns.zh: 确切地说，把甜甜圈带来。

turns.speaker: Chris Miller
turns.en: I must be old, I don't know that anybody uses bringing the donuts now anymore.
turns.zh: 我一定是老了，我不知道现在还有人带甜甜圈了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No, we had Ken on the podcast, we talked about it. We asked, what is the digital version of that when everyone's working remote? I think that's something that even if you're a brand new PM you come across soon enough. And then the other piece there, I really love this metaphor of scraping your knees because I find that to be so important to becoming a PM is you think you could just read these things, take some courses and you got this, and you're not going to mess up, but I find that messing up is so important in helping to learn to do the job because like you said, there's relationships and people and changing plans and leaders, and it's just like you're not going to get it right and you learn how to deal with all these things by messing it up. (00:22:01): So, I super agree with that, and even though you said it's easier not to learn to be a PM, it's still I think important to scrape your knees a number of times for you to actually learn to do the job. Along those lines, what did you find was most helpful to you to learn the craft of product management in the first few years? What do you think back to like, "Oh, that was really helpful," other than just doing it messing up, sometimes getting it right?"
turns.zh: 不，我们有肯在播客上，我们讨论过它。我们问，当每个人都远程工作时，数字版本是什么？我认为即使您是一位全新的产品经理，您也很快就会遇到这一点。然后另一篇文章，我真的很喜欢这个擦膝盖的比喻，因为我发现对于成为一名产品经理来说如此重要的是你认为你可以阅读这些东西，参加一些课程，然后你就得到了这个，你不会搞砸，但我发现搞砸对于帮助学习完成这项工作非常重要，因为就像你说的，有人际关系和人员以及不断变化的计划和领导者，就像你不会把事情做好一样，你学会如何处理所有的事情把这些事情搞砸了。 (00:22:01)：所以，我非常同意这一点，尽管你说不学习成为一名产品经理会更容易，但我仍然认为，为了真正学会做这份工作，多次擦膝盖仍然很重要。沿着这些思路，您发现在最初几年里什么对您学习产品管理技巧最有帮助？除了把事情搞砸，有时把事情做对之外，你觉得“哦，这真的很有帮助”，还有什么？

turns.speaker: Chris Miller
turns.en: So, my first product management job/mission was working on a B2B2C product, and there's a lot of unique challenges that came with that. Our customer was not the end user of our product. We sold into institutions who then white labeled our product and then resold it to the end customer. And so at the end of the day, our customers own the relationship with the end user and not us, and so-
turns.zh: 因此，我的第一份产品管理工作/任务是开发 B2B2C 产品，随之而来的是许多独特的挑战。我们的客户不是我们产品的最终用户。我们向机构出售产品，然后这些机构将我们的产品贴上白色标签，然后将其转售给最终客户。所以归根结底，我们的客户拥有与最终用户的关系，而不是我们，所以-

turns.speaker: Chris Miller
turns.en: ... own the relationship with the end user and not us. And so, the challenges that that created were that there was a lot of distance between us and the voice of the end user. And we ended up building a lot of things to satisfy the buyer and the customer, but not necessarily the end user. And that's challenging because you don't necessarily know whether you're building something to get a contract signed, or you're building something that's going to delight the person using it at the end of the day, or provide magical value. And so, I think I probably shipped a lot of bad product those years, if I'm being completely honest. I don't know that I would look back at what I shipped back then or what we shipped back then, and say they were the best possible solutions or best possible product. (00:23:47): It wasn't until I got my second product management job where it really was an inflection point, where I was like, "Oh, got it. This is what this is supposed to look and feel like."
turns.zh: ...拥有与最终用户的关系，而不是我们。因此，这带来的挑战是我们与最终用户的声音之间存在很大的距离。我们最终构建了很多东西来满足买家和客户，但不一定是最终用户。这很有挑战性，因为你不一定知道你正在构建的东西是否是为了签署合同，或者你正在构建的东西最终会让使用它的人感到高兴，或者提供神奇的价值。所以，如果我完全诚实的话，我想那些年我可能运送了很多劣质产品。我不知道我会回顾我当时运送的东西或我们当时运送的东西，并说它们是最好的解决方案或最好的产品。 (00:23:47)：直到我找到第二份产品管理工作，这才真正成为一个转折点，我当时想，“哦，明白了。这就是它应该看起来和感觉的样子。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Where was that? Was that with Keeper?
turns.zh: 那是哪里？是和Keeper一起的吗？

turns.speaker: Chris Miller
turns.en: I was working at a fitness technology company, and the person who really I would say changed my entire paradigm of what product management is supposed to be, someone I know you know, Fareed Mosavat, who I believe was on the pod-
turns.zh: 我当时在一家健身技术公司工作，我想说的是，那个人真正改变了我对产品管理的整个范式，我认识的人，你也知道，法里德·莫萨瓦特（Fareed Mosavat），我相信他就在 Pod 上——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Ooh. Absolutely.

turns.speaker: Chris Miller
turns.en: ... last October. Shout out to Fareed if you're listening. Fareed is a good friend and mentor, and he really helped me level up. And what was interesting about those years is it was the first time I'd really gotten to work on a product where it was a freemium B2C run-tracking app. And so, we spent a lot of time talking to users directly, and a lot of guerrilla user research techniques. Literally, sometimes going outside and just talking to runners in passing to understand what were the challenges in finding motivation, and why do they choose running assistance, running applications in the first place? And so, just that having that deep connection to the customer and not feeling like you're being kept at arms' distance was eyeopening. I was like, "Oh, I didn't know that it could be like this." (00:25:12): And then, the second thing that we had at our disposal that changed the game for me was access to a huge user data set. And so, having data at scale to drive decisions, being able to know that if we make a change, we can prove causation from a business impact standpoint or a customer delight or engagement standpoint. And so, it was almost like I didn't realize I was blind until... Or you didn't realize you weren't seeing in color. It's like that scene in The Wizard of Oz where they land on Oz, and all of a sudden, everything's in Technicolor. And you're like, "Oh, my gosh, I can actually make informed decisions about what I'm shipping." (00:25:56): And having a level of rigor around that and really being forced to articulate a hypothesis and have a point of view on what the outcomes might be before you actually build something, were all sort of, I would say, behaviors and just philosophy around product discipline that I learned from Fareed and that group of folks that I worked with closely during those years. And that was, I think the... I consider that to be when I really became a product manager.
turns.zh: ...去年十月。如果你在听的话，请大声向法里德喊叫。法里德是我的好朋友和导师，他确实帮助我提升了水平。那些年的有趣之处在于，这是我第一次真正开始开发免费增值 B2C 跑步跟踪应用程序的产品。因此，我们花了很多时间直接与用户交谈，并使用了很多游击式用户研究技术。从字面上看，有时走到外面，只是顺便与跑步者交谈，以了解寻找动力的挑战是什么，以及为什么他们首先选择跑步辅助、运行应用程序？因此，与客户建立深厚的联系，而不是感觉自己与客户保持着距离，这真是令人大开眼界。我当时想，“哦，我不知道事情会是这样的。” (00:25:12)：然后，我们可以使用的第二件事改变了我的游戏规则，那就是访问庞大的用户数据集。因此，拥有大规模数据来推动决策，能够知道如果我们做出改变，我们可以从业务影响的角度或客户满意度或参与度的角度证明因果关系。所以，就好像我没有意识到自己是盲人，直到……或者你没有意识到你看不到颜色。这就像《绿野仙踪》中的场景，他们降落在奥兹国，突然之间，一切都变成了彩色的。你会想，“哦，天哪，我实际上可以对我要运送的东西做出明智的决定。” (00:25:56)：对此有一定程度的严格性，并且在真正构建某些东西之前确实被迫阐明一个假设并对结果可能会是什么有自己的看法，我想说的是，我从法里德和那些年与我密切合作的那群人那里学到了围绕产品纪律的行为和哲学。那是，我认为……我认为那是我真正成为一名产品经理的时候。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's two things I want to highlight there that, again, super resonate. One is just whenever I talk to customers, I'm like, "Why don't I do this more often?" Because every time it's like, "Wow, I had no idea how big of a problem that was. Why don't I do this all the time?" And then, you don't again. And then, you do it months later and you're like, "Oh, my god, I learned so much again." And so, I think if you're listening and you're just like... Maybe just go talk to a customer today.
turns.zh: 我想强调两件事，再次引起强烈共鸣。一是每当我与客户交谈时，我都会想，“为什么我不经常这样做呢？”因为每次都会这样，“哇，我不知道这是一个多大的问题。为什么我不一直这样做呢？”然后，你就不再这样了。然后，几个月后你这样做了，你会想，“哦，天哪，我又学到了很多东西。”因此，我认为如果您正在倾听并且您就像……也许今天就去与客户交谈。

turns.speaker: Chris Miller
turns.en: Talk to customers, and we also learned a lot from talking to people who we wanted to be customers but were not, right? And people who had either broken up with our product or evaluated it and never fell in love with it in the first place. And so, I think every PM struggles with time management and it feels like you need 60 hours in a day to get through your weekly checklist, or 60 hours in a week, excuse me. But finding time to just talk to people. Even today, I have a lot of friends who are entrepreneurs or small business owners, and some use HubSpot, some don't. But I usually tend to really enjoy my conversations with people who decided not to use HubSpot and to really try to unpack what drove that decision. (00:27:40): Was it as calculated, as I think sometimes we can all maybe assume that some of these decisions are? And then you often learn that they're sometimes kind of emotional, really instinctual and visceral and maybe connected to brands more than they even connected to product. And there's a lot of things that I think when you're in the proverbial digital conference room with your team, trying to understand what makes your users tick, you're just like, "We're actually just..." We're illogical humans at the end of the day at our core, and that all rides on decisions people make in the day-to-day. And it doesn't change, necessarily, when they're engaging with your product. As much as we love it to be perfect science, so that we can moneyball the system, if you will.
turns.zh: 与客户交谈，我们也从与那些我们想成为客户但实际上不是客户的人交谈中学到了很多东西，对吧？那些要么已经放弃了我们的产品，要么评估了我们的产品但从未爱上它的人。所以，我认为每个 PM 都在时间管理上挣扎，感觉就像你每天需要 60 小时才能完成每周检查清单，或者一周需要 60 小时，对不起。但要找时间与人交谈。即使在今天，我还有很多企业家或小企业主朋友，有些使用 HubSpot，有些则不使用。但我通常很喜欢与那些决定不使用 HubSpot 的人进行对话，并真正尝试找出推动这一决定的原因。 (00:27:40)：是否像我认为有时我们都可以假设其中一些决定是经过计算的那样？然后你经常会发现，他们有时是情绪化的、真正本能的、发自内心的，可能与品牌的联系甚至比与产品的联系还要多。我认为，当你和你的团队一起在众所周知的数字会议室里，试图了解是什么让你的用户感兴趣时，你会想，“我们实际上只是……”归根结底，我们都是不合逻辑的人类，而这一切都取决于人们在日常中做出的决定。当他们与你的产品互动时，它不一定会改变。尽管我们非常喜欢它是完美的科学，所以如果你愿意的话，我们可以通过这个系统来赚钱。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It reminds me of a story where we were doing some user research on a booking feature with an Airbnb. And we went to Paris to do these really in-depth user research studies. We were behind one-way mirrors and all that stuff. And we were trying to figure out why hosts weren't connecting Facebook to their account. This is like, I don't know, five, six years ago. Because it gave them so much access to where their friends are traveling and reviews and all these things. And especially, in France, they were just like, "I don't trust Facebook." And this was before it became a big thing in the US. They're just like, "I don't trust... I don't want them to have any of my data." "But look at all this power you get." They're like, "No, I don't care. I don't trust it." And-
turns.zh: 这让我想起一个故事，我们当时正在对 Airbnb 的预订功能进行一些用户研究。我们去了巴黎进行这些非常深入的用户研究。我们在单向镜子之类的东西后面。我们试图弄清楚为什么房东没有将 Facebook 连接到他们的帐户。这就像，我不知道，五六年前。因为它让他们可以方便地了解朋友的旅行地点、评论以及所有这些信息。尤其是在法国，他们的反应是“我不信任 Facebook”。这是在它在美国成为一件大事之前。他们就像是，“我不相信......我不想让他们拥有我的任何数据。” “但是看看你所获得的所有力量。”他们会说，“不，我不在乎。我不相信它。”和-

turns.speaker: Chris Miller
turns.en: Yeah, that's why talking to customers is so... You could have all the usage data in the world, that's going to tell you what's actually happening in your product, but it doesn't tell you why. It will never explain the why behind a behavior that you can track through events firing. And so, that's why that sort of proximity to the customer and directing that sort of relentless curiosity towards the qualitative stuff is so, so important because you just learn things that are just sometimes really unintuitive or are blind spots because we're often not the people we're building product for.
turns.zh: 是的，这就是为什么与客户交谈是如此......您可以拥有世界上所有的使用数据，这将告诉您产品中实际发生的情况，但它不会告诉您原因。它永远不会解释您可以通过事件触发跟踪的行为背后的原因。因此，这就是为什么这种与客户的接近以及对定性事物的那种不懈的好奇心是如此非常重要，因为你只是学到有时非常不直观或盲点的东西，因为我们通常不是我们正在为其构建产品的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely. I want to shift talking about HubSpot the business, but one more last thing I wanted to highlight from what you just shared, which is a really good insight is you shared that your biggest inflection in your career was a manager, Fareed in this case, who helped you learn the craft and develop your skills, and that's the exact experience I had too. Just one specific manager changed everything for me. And that feels like a recurring theme to a lot of people, just having one person that really spends the time to help you learn and correct you when you're making mistakes and all that. So, if folks are wondering maybe why am I not learning enough or why is my care stagnating? See if you can just find... Easier said than done, but oftentimes it just takes one person to change everything.
turns.zh: 绝对地。我想把话题转移到 HubSpot 业务上，但我想从你刚才分享的内容中强调最后一件事，这是一个非常好的见解，你分享了你职业生涯中最大的转折点是一名经理，在这个例子中是法里德，他帮助你学习工艺和发展你的技能，这也是我的经历。仅仅一位特定的经理就改变了我的一切。对于很多人来说，这感觉就像是一个反复出现的主题，只要有一个人真正花时间帮助你学习并在你犯错误时纠正你等等。那么，如果人们想知道为什么我学得不够或者为什么我的护理停滞不前？看看你是否能找到……说起来容易做起来难，但通常只需要一个人就能改变一切。

turns.speaker: Chris Miller
turns.en: It gets into sort of a conversation about the difference between a manager and a mentor, versus a sponsor and an advocate. Mentors are great, don't get me wrong. I have a ton of people that I would consider to be mentors, but when I think about the people in my life, who... The time that they donated to me, the time that they volunteered to me and for me, calling them mentors, I think sells what they were very short. And I would actually describe those folks as being sponsors and advocates, people who were willing to put up capital, whether that's professional, social capital to bet on you. (00:30:56): I mean, truth be told, when I interviewed with Fareed that first time, I think back to the interview and I think I bombed it. I actually don't think I would've hired me back then. And I remember the answers I gave to some of those questions, and I think they were good, but I don't think they were certainly great. And I imagine that there was something in there where the decision maker, who was Fareed said, "I think I can make something out of this." And I think being willing to invest in someone and finding people who are willing to invest in you is what really matters. And finding people who are willing to, again, put something up for you, whether that be whatever kind of capital it is. When I think about true gasoline on the career fire, it's finding mentors, but it's also finding sponsors and advocates.
turns.zh: 它涉及到关于经理和导师、发起人和倡导者之间区别的对话。导师们都很棒，别误会我的意思。我有很多人，我认为他们是导师，但当我想到我生命中的人时，他们……他们为我捐赠的时间，他们自愿为我和为我服务的时间，称他们为导师，我认为出售他们非常短暂的东西。我实际上将这些人描述为赞助商和倡导者，愿意投入资金的人，无论是专业的还是社会的资本来押注于你。 (00:30:56)：我的意思是，说实话，当我第一次采访法里德时，我回想起那次采访，我认为我搞砸了。事实上，我认为当时不会雇用我。我记得我对其中一些问题的回答，我认为它们很好，但我不认为它们一定很棒。我想决策者法里德说：“我想我可以从中做点什么。”我认为愿意投资某人并找到愿意投资你的人才是真正重要的。再次找到愿意为你提供一些东西的人，无论那是什么类型的资本。当我想到真正的职业火力时，它是寻找导师，但它也是寻找赞助商和倡导者。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything that you think you did right to help find mentors and sponsors and advocates for people that are thinking about, "Hey, I need this. How do I help myself in the same way?" Is there something you did that helped people get excited to help you?
turns.zh: 您认为自己做对了哪些事情来帮助那些正在思考“嘿，我需要这个。我如何以同样的方式帮助自己？”的人找到导师、赞助商和倡导者？你做过什么事情让人们很乐意帮助你吗？

turns.speaker: Chris Miller
turns.en: Something I think I certainly continue to work on, but really, putting ego aside and embracing not knowing stuff and embracing not being good at stuff, and not feeling self-conscious about that and letting the desire to be the best at something or at least be great at something overpower the fear of being inadequate at something. And I played sports growing up, and so I like being coached. I can take hard feedback, and I like it because if I get better feedback than the people I'm competing against, I think I can beat them over time if I work hard enough. (00:32:42): And so, I think just taking that mentality with me into product management, I think has helped me build bridges with people who don't owe me anything, right? People who don't necessarily need to be invested in me at all, but who might get delight out of it somehow. And I don't know exactly how that works and the calculus that goes on in folks' brains, but at least what's within my control is how I can show up in the context of those relationships and really embrace even the hardest, ugliest feedback and hope that I can extract something from it that'll make me better at the end of the day.
turns.zh: 我想我当然会继续努力，但实际上，把自我放在一边，拥抱不知道的东西，拥抱不擅长的东西，不要对此感到不自在，让在某事上做到最好或至少在某事上表现出色的愿望压倒对某事不足的恐惧。我从小就参加体育运动，所以我喜欢接受教练的指导。我可以接受严格的反馈，我喜欢它，因为如果我得到比我的竞争对手更好的反馈，我想如果我足够努力的话，随着时间的推移我可以击败他们。 (00:32:42)：所以，我认为将这种心态带入产品管理中，我认为帮助我与那些不欠我任何东西的人建立了桥梁，对吗？这些人根本不需要对我进行投资，但可能会以某种方式从中获得乐趣。我不知道它到底是如何运作的，也不知道人们大脑中是如何进行计算的，但至少在我的控制范围内，我可以如何在这些关系的背景下表现出来，并真正接受最艰难、最丑陋的反馈，并希望我能从中提取一些东西，让我在一天结束时变得更好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that advice. Makes me think about Jules Walter's advice, which I've referenced many times on this podcast now, where his tip is when people are giving you feedback, just be like, "Thank you so much for that feedback," even though you're melting inside and just completely disagree with what they're telling you.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个建议。让我想起了朱尔斯·沃尔特（Jules Walter）的建议，我现在已经在这个播客中多次引用过这个建议，他的建议是，当人们向你提供反馈时，只需说“非常感谢你的反馈”，即使你内心融化并且完全不同意他们告诉你的内容。

turns.speaker: Chris Miller
turns.en: Yeah, shout out to Jules. Jules is also someone who has been generous with me in the past in terms of giving time when I've needed help with stuff. Also, a great episode you did with Jules.
turns.zh: 是的，向朱尔斯大声喊叫。朱尔斯过去也对我很慷慨，当我需要帮助时，他会给予我时间。另外，你和朱尔斯一起拍的很棒的一集。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, many people have said what you just said about Jules, about how helpful he is been to them. So, clearly, a class act to that guy, maybe we'll have to bring him back.
turns.zh: 所以，很多人都说了你刚才所说的关于朱尔斯的事情，关于他对他们有多大的帮助。所以，显然，这对那个人来说是一种集体行为，也许我们必须把他带回来。

turns.speaker: Chris Miller
turns.en: Would love that.
turns.zh: 会喜欢的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. V2 Jules. So, let's shift to HubSpot the business, which is a pretty incredible success story. From what my notes, it's worth something like $30 billion now as a business. turns.zh: 是的。 V2朱尔斯。那么，让我们把业务转向 HubSpot，这是一个非常令人难以置信的成功故事。根据我的记录，它现在的价值约为 300 亿美元。它已经存在了 17 年。我认为仍在增长，年增长率约为 30%。最有趣的是，Okta 最近发布了一份非常有趣的报告，他们查看了人们使用哪些工具进行身份验证的数据，结果表明 HubSpot 可能是世界上增长速度第五快的软件产品。我不知道这是不是真的，但感觉是真的，因为所有其他公司在那里都有意义。所以，你不必确认或否认这一点，但显然 HubSpot 的情况进展顺利。我很好奇到底是什么让 HubSpot 如此特别、独特和成功，是 HubSpot 与其他公司相比的独特之处？

turns.speaker: Chris Miller
turns.en: There's a lot in there. I can speak to the things that have resonated most deeply with me in my time there. The first is legitimate customer obsession. It's not marketing, it's legitimate, right? I've witnessed fierce and passionate debates internally that the root of what the people in the debate were really trying to unpack was what was the best thing for the customer. And so, really having that be central to our dogma and how we think about the business and why the company exists in the first place, really walking the walk there is something that I don't know that that's true everywhere. (00:35:39): I mean, I've certainly worked at places where that hasn't been true, and there's a lot of factors that can lead to those trade-off decisions at times. Like is this the right thing for the business, the right thing for the customer? Being really challenging. I think just sort of having that customer centricity really baked into the DNA of the company makes those decisions, maybe not easier, but at least you can have more conviction around the why behind the decision at the end of the day. Another thing that I think makes HubSpot-
turns.zh: 里面有很多东西。我可以谈论我在那里的时光中最能引起我共鸣的事情。首先是合理的客户迷恋。这不是营销，这是合法的，对吗？我目睹了内部激烈而激烈的辩论，辩论中的人们真正试图解开的根源是什么对客户来说是最好的。因此，真正将其作为我们信条的核心，以及我们如何看待业务以及公司存在的首要原因，真正做到这一点，我不知道这在任何地方都是如此。 (00:35:39)：我的意思是，我确实在一些不真实的地方工作过，有时有很多因素可能导致做出这些权衡决定。这对企业来说是正确的事情吗？对客户来说是正确的事情吗？真的很有挑战性。我认为，只要将以客户为中心的理念真正融入到公司的 DNA 中，就能做出这些决策，也许并不容易，但至少你可以在一天结束时更加确信决策背后的原因。我认为 HubSpot 的另一件事是——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Before you actually move on to the next one, I want to spend a little time on this one because I think people hear this and they're like, "Yes, okay, we're going to be customer obsessed." And then, you have to make these hard decisions. Look at this experiment, it's going to grow our revenue 1%, but it's not really going to make the customer's life easier. How do you actually make this real? And there may be an example where you have to trade off growth versus we need to make sure the customer is getting what they need or making the customer happy to make it a little more real even.
turns.zh: 在你真正进入下一个之前，我想花一点时间在这个上，因为我认为人们听到这个并且他们会说，“是的，好吧，我们将成为客户至上的人。”然后，你必须做出这些艰难的决定。看看这个实验，它会让我们的收入增长 1%，但它并不能真正让客户的生活变得更轻松。你如何真正实现这一点？可能有一个例子，你必须权衡增长与我们需要确保客户得到他们需要的东西，或者让客户高兴地让它变得更加真实。

turns.speaker: Chris Miller
turns.en: One, I think that's a really fantastic, maybe not counterpoint, but thing to call out. My point of view here is that oftentimes it's a function of what's the time horizon that the company uses as their sort of baseline for assessing decisions? And typically, when you're making decisions that could be described as hostile towards your customers, but a net positive for the business, you're probably not thinking long-term enough, right? Because there's no possible way, unless you have completely cornered a market and there is no competition whatsoever, that you could continually be hostile towards your customers and grow, right? At some point, that's going to catch up. (00:37:25): And so, oftentimes I think it's the tension of what do we need to do in the short term to survive? Versus long-term, where are we going? What's the path that we're actually charting? Is I think the true tension. But if you're making decisions that might have lasting impact that are customer hostile, I think that's a really dangerous path to kind of go down. And so, having, I think, the discipline or the bravery or the courage, whatever, to I think focus on not necessarily tomorrow or the day after, and really think about two, three, four years from now, what are the outcomes we're trying to drive and what are the decisions we need to make in the interim that are going to lead to that outcome?
